GUI usage

The web interface offers the same analyses as the terminal interface in a browser. Start it from the project folder with:

python run.py web

The console prints the address, http://127.0.0.1:5000/ by default; open it in a browser. The Settings page (or the Settings menu of the terminal interface) changes the address and port for the next start; --host and --port change them for one run. Stop the server with Ctrl+C in its console; a loaded interactive session is released when the server stops.

Security. The server reads any local path you type and can load any model, so keep it on the loopback address, which is the default. Do not give it a public address, and do not expose the port on a network or through a tunnel; when it is not on a loopback address, the console and the Settings page warn that other machines can reach it. The server answers only requests addressed to it by a loopback name (localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]) or by the address it listens on; listening on 0.0.0.0 or ::, it also answers this machine's own addresses (those its host name resolves to, and the one of its default route), so another machine reaches it as http://<IP of this machine>:<port>/. Any other name is refused (DNS rebinding). It refuses state-changing requests coming from another site, and sends a strict content security policy; saved reports are shown with a policy that allows no script at all. Token texts and model metadata are treated as hostile and escaped wherever they are shown.

Layout. A sidebar on the left links to every page, grouped into sections: Home on its own; a Tools section (Weight Diff, Entropy Analysis, Token Shifts, Vocabulary & Embeddings, Hub Lineage, Provenance, Behaviour Probe); a Reports section (Tools, which opens the saved reports, and Analysis, a placeholder detailed later); a System section (Environment, Settings); and Documentation on its own. Tools, Reports and System are collapsible headers, not links: click one to open or shut its list, and the section holding the current page opens on its own. A divider sits above Reports, System and Documentation. In a window narrower than 1400 pixels the pages use the full width: the sidebar is replaced by a bar at the top holding a menu button, the application name and the name of the current page. The menu button slides the same sidebar in over the page; it closes when you pick a page, click outside it, press Esc or widen the window. On a phone-sized screen the bar drops the application name. When a feature cannot run on this machine, its page shows a red banner This feature is unavailable on this machine: with the missing packages, and its run buttons are disabled.

Menu-bar status and system readout. The foot of the sidebar shows a live status chip and a short system readout. The chip reads OK (green) when the server is idle, Running (orange, blinking) while an analysis is running, and Error (red) when the most recent analysis failed — the same job the finish notifications track, so the chip reflects it wherever you are. Below it, four lines give the address the server listens on (IP:port, resolved to one of this machine's own addresses when it is bound to every interface), the available and total RAM, the GPU name (or N/A with no CUDA device), and the available and total VRAM (or N/A). The RAM and VRAM figures refresh every few seconds, so the readout tracks what the machine has free while an analysis loads models.

Model fields. Every field that takes a model works the same way. Type a local folder, a .gguf file or a Hub id (quotes around a pasted path are removed), then click Detect or press Enter. Two aids help fill the field: as you type what looks like a Hub id, a drop-down suggests matching repositories from the Hugging Face Hub (it stays empty when there is no connection); and Browse… opens a navigator of this machine's folders and the .gguf files on them, where you move through folders, switch drive, go ↑ Up, and either Use this folder or click a .gguf file — the choice fills the field and is detected at once. The line under the field says what was found, for example LoRA adapter (local) · declared base Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, or why the reference cannot be used, in red. Depending on what was found, more controls appear:

  • Checkpoint: a training output folder lists its checkpoints; choosing one replaces the reference and detects it.
  • GGUF file: a folder or repository with several GGUF files lists them, the first marked (most precise) and selected by default.
  • Adapter base override: for a LoRA adapter, the base it is applied to. Leave it empty to use the base the adapter declares (shown as a placeholder); fill it when the adapter declares none.

You do not have to click Detect: the run buttons detect every model field that has not been detected yet, and refuse to start until all of them are usable. Editing a reference clears its detection.

Running an analysis. A run button shows a progress panel with the analysis title, a bar (moving stripes while the total is not known), the current step and a Cancel button. The page asks the server for progress every second. Cancel asks the analysis to stop at its next checkpoint; the panel then shows Cancelled.. A failure is shown in red in place of the results. One analysis runs at a time, across every page and browser tab: starting another while one runs is refused with a notification naming the running process and a Go to it link to its page.

Leaving and coming back. An analysis keeps running on the server while you move to other pages. Returning to the page that started it picks the run back up: the progress panel resumes if it is still running, or the finished view appears if it completed while you were away. Wherever you are when a process finishes, a notification appears in the top-right corner (<Tool> finished, or failed / cancelled); it is shown once. The interactive Behaviour Probe session is not tracked this way — its loaded models are restored from the server when you reopen the page.

Results and downloads. When an analysis succeeds, its report is saved and the input panel(s) stay collapsed behind a short finished view: a verdict banner summarising the result and two buttons — Open report opens the complete saved report in a new tab (with its downloads and every detail), and New analysis reopens the inputs at their defaults and clears the result. The verdict banner is coloured by the result (grey within the baseline, blue, amber or red as the evidence strengthens, green for a confirmed provenance match) with a caps heading and a one-line headline carrying the key numbers; a few supporting lines may follow. The complete tables — heaviest tensors, token projections, per-prompt KL and the rest — are in the saved report, not the live page. The small button at the end of a table row (in the Behaviour interactive session and the Hub Lineage discovery) copies its main value to the clipboard. Tokens are shown as chips with their whitespace made visible: ␣ for a space, \n for a newline, ∅ for an empty token; hovering a chip shows its token id and score. A z-score badge is green from 3 up, amber from 1 up, and grey below, where it is noise.

Home

The home page is the Analyse a Model workflow: it runs every tool on a model and reads a suspicion verdict. The navigation sidebar reaches the individual tools, the reports and the system pages.

Input: Model to analyse, and an optional Source model (the model it is claimed to derive from; leave it empty to discover the source with Provenance). The Workflow panel's toggles choose what runs: verify a given source with Provenance, search the Hub when none is given, the four weight analyses — Weight Diff, Entropy Analysis, Token Shifts and Vocabulary & Embeddings — and the Behaviour Probe (off by default, with an optional prompts box). When you detect the model to analyse, the analyses relevant for its format are pre-selected (the Entropy Analysis off for every format, the Token Shifts off for bitsandbytes models, the Vocabulary & Embeddings off for a LoRA adapter); turn any on or off to override. A disabled tool reads as "not run" in the results. An Advanced options panel exposes the per-tool parameters and explicit Provenance candidates. Button: Run analysis (disabled, with the reason, when the weight tools are unavailable here).

While the analysis runs, the Model and Workflow panels fold away to make room (click the chevron in a panel's header to open it again) and a step tracker shows the workflow — Source, Weight Diff, Entropy, Token Shifts, Vocabulary & Embeddings, Behaviour and Report — colouring each step as the run moves through it: grey for a step still pending, orange for the step running now, green for a finished one, and a dashed grey for a step skipped because its toggle was off.

When the analysis finishes, the Model and Workflow panels stay collapsed and the page shows the executive summary only, laid out exactly as in the saved report:

  • A verdict banner coloured by risk (clean green, low blue, elevated amber, high red) with its caps heading and the headline.
  • Executive Summary table: the risk and confidence badges, how the source was established, the markers (one line per flagged tool, or a note that every analysis stayed within its baseline), and — for a medium or high flag — an Impact and an Example line spelling out what the modification could do.

Two buttons sit above it: Open report opens the complete saved report in a new tab (the report is listed under Reports > Analysis, not Tools, with its own downloads and the per-tool detail); New analysis reopens the Model and Workflow panels at their default values and clears the previous result.

Weight Diff

How much every tensor of a tuned model moved from its base.

Input: Base model (the reference the tuned model is compared with) and Tuned model (full or merged weights, a LoRA adapter or checkpoint, GGUF or bitsandbytes). Button: Compare weights.

Finished view: a risk verdict banner graded from the shape of the change — concentrated in a few tensors (targeted) or broad (continued training), and WITHIN BASELINE for a quantized comparison with nothing beyond its noise floor — with a headline giving how many of the compared tensors changed. The heaviest-tensor table, the per-layer change and the full counts are in the saved report.

Entropy Analysis

How the entropy of the last layers' weights shifts from a source model to a fine-tune.

Input: Source model (the reference, which fixes the layer count and the scope) and Tuned model (full or merged weights, a LoRA adapter or checkpoint, GGUF or bitsandbytes), then Last blocks to examine and Histogram bins. Button: Analyse entropy.

Finished view: a risk verdict banner graded from the spectral-entropy shift against the random-update null (a drop well beyond the null reads as restructuring; a shift within the quantization noise floor reads as a dequantization artefact), with a headline giving that z. The null comparison, the most-shifted tensors and the per-layer shift are in the saved report.

Token Shifts

The heaviest weight updates, read through the vocabulary.

Input: Base model (it also provides the tokenizer and the vocabulary matrices), Tuned model, Updates to project (the heaviest 2-D updates by leading singular value, default 10, 1 to 200) and Tokens listed (at each end of a direction and per embedding matrix, default 15, 1 to 100). Button: Analyse shifts; Enter in a number field also starts it.

Finished view: a risk verdict banner graded from the peak token-set alignment of the heaviest updates against the shuffle null (an update that behaves like a trigger on a token set), with a headline giving that peak z and a line with how many tensors changed. The heaviest updates with their projected token ends, and the moved embedding rows, are in the saved report.

Hub Lineage

The declared parents and children of a Hugging Face model, then the token-shift comparison of the pairs you choose. This page works in two steps.

Input: Model (a Hub repository id, with the same Hub drop-down suggestions as the model fields), Mode (Parents and children, Parents only or Children only), Maximum variants (children kept, the most downloaded first, default 5, 1 to 50) and Maximum size (GB) (larger full-weight children are skipped, default 8). Button: Discover relatives; Enter in a field also starts it.

The Discovery panel then shows the target and its kind, and up to four tables: Parents (relation and repository), Children (repository, relation, downloads), Comparable pairs (parent, child, kind, with a Use checkbox, all ticked) and Skipped (repository and reason), then the notes. Untick the pairs you do not want and click Analyse the selected pairs.

When you analyse the selected pairs, the Input and Discovery panels fold away (click a chevron to reopen one) and the page shows a lineage summary: how many of the chosen pairs compared, the strongest shift found (σ and tensor) and any pairs that failed, above the Open report and New analysis buttons. The per-pair detail is in the saved report. A new discovery reopens the panels and clears the summary.

Provenance

Which candidate model a suspect's weights derive from: screened by raw similarity, then compared in depth with basis-invariant circuits.

Input:

  • Suspect model: the model under investigation (full weights, an adapter, GGUF or bitsandbytes).
  • Candidate parents: local paths or Hub ids, one per line (commas also separate them), optional, at most 50. Declared bases are always added. Ctrl+Enter in this box starts the analysis.
  • Search the Hub for same-type candidates: on by default. When it is on, Search text replaces the search by model type (leave it empty to keep it; it offers the same Hub drop-down suggestions as the model fields), and Include models that declare a base (off by default) also admits fine-tunes and instruct models.
  • Layers compared in depth: compared tensor by tensor from layer 0, default 1, 1 to 64.
  • Top k: screened candidates compared in depth, default 3, 1 to 40.

Button: Find the provenance.

Finished view: a verdict banner for the best weight-level match — the rank verdict as its heading (green for identical weights or a same-basis derivative, amber for a related model or a transformed basis, grey for no match) — with a headline naming the best candidate and its median raw cosine, and a line giving how many candidates were gathered, compatible and screened. The ranking, the screen and the skipped candidates are in the saved report.

Behaviour Probe

Where the next-token predictions of both models differ.

The Models panel holds Base model (full weights, GGUF or bitsandbytes, not an adapter), Tuned model (an adapter or checkpoint is accepted) and Mode: Batch probe on a prompts file or Interactive session. The mode shows the matching panel below.

Batch probe. Drop a prompts file on the drop zone, or click browse files; change file picks another. Accepted files are .txt (one prompt per line), .json and .jsonl (strings, or objects holding the JSON field, or chat-format {"messages": [...]} records), up to 2,097,152 bytes, the limit shown in the drop zone. The other fields are JSON field (default question), Maximum prompts (default 50, 1 to 10,000), Tokens generated by both models (0 for none, up to 1024) and the switch Wrap prompts in the chat template (on). Button: Run the probe.

When the batch probe finishes, the Models and Batch probe panels fold away and the page shows a risk verdict banner graded from the mean prediction divergence against the control-prompt null (far beyond the controls reads as a targeted change), with a headline giving the mean KL, the control mean and the z, and lines with the maximum KL and the number of positions. The per-prompt table, the hottest positions, the promoted and suppressed tokens and the generations are in the saved report.

Interactive session. The badge says whether models are loaded. Load models loads both models once (with a progress panel); only one session exists at a time, and loading a new pair unloads the previous one. Once loaded, the panel gives the models, where each was placed and in which precision, and the number of prompts analysed; Unload releases them. The controls are:

  • Prompt, a text box (at most 20,000 characters); Ctrl+Enter compares both models on it.
  • Positions and tokens listed: default 15, 1 to 100.
  • Tokens generated (0 = none): up to 1024.
  • Wrap the prompt in the chat template: on by default.
  • Compare runs the prompt; it cannot be cancelled, and waits for both models.
  • Save report probes every prompt of the session on the loaded pair, with the control prompts, saves the report, shows its report bar under the buttons and the risk summary below, as for a batch.

The History lists the prompts compared, newest first. Each entry shows its mean KL, max KL and positions, the prompt, the next-token predictions of both models, the hottest positions, the promoted and suppressed tokens, and the generations when enabled. The session lives on the server: after a page reload it is shown again as it was.

Reports

The sidebar's Reports section holds two pages: Tools, the reports of the individual tools, and Analysis, the reports of the Analyse a Model workflow. Each lists its own reports, newest first, in a Saved reports panel; the reports folder is shown at the top right, with a Refresh button. Both tables open with a Model column, the name of the analysed model (a Hub id in full, a local path as its file name). Tools then shows Analysis (the tool) and Created; Analysis shows a Format column, how its weights are stored (safetensors, GGUF, LoRA adapter or bitsandbytes), then Created and Risk, the workflow's risk-level tag. Both end with Size and Actions:

  • View opens the HTML report in a new tab.
  • HTML and JSON download report.html and report.json.
  • Delete asks for confirmation (Delete or Cancel, Escape also cancels), then removes the report's files. This cannot be undone.

On a narrow window (below the drawer breakpoint), these action buttons show icons instead of their labels, each with a tooltip naming the action.

The reports are the same as in the terminal interface.

Environment

What this machine can do, the same report as python run.py check, in three tables. System gives the version, the platform, Python, the GPU and CUDA (torch), which says whether the installed torch can use the GPU. Features says for each feature whether it is available and, if not, which packages it needs. Packages gives the installed version of each package, or not installed. Refresh observes the machine again, for instance after installing a package; the rest of the interface picks up the change when its pages are reloaded.

Settings

The Web server panel holds the Listening IP address and the Port the server listens on, with a default badge when they are the defaults and a Default: 127.0.0.1:5000 line below. 127.0.0.1 keeps the interface on this machine; 0.0.0.0 listens on every network interface. The address must belong to this machine, and the port be a whole number from 1 to 65,535.

  • Save (or Enter in either field) stores them; a notification gives the new address, an invalid value is shown in red and nothing is stored.
  • Restore the default stores the defaults; it is disabled when they are already in place.

A change to the address applies the next time the server starts: the running server keeps its address. When the address is not a loopback one, an amber warning says that other machines will reach the server, which has no authentication.

The Directories panel holds the Report directory, where reports are saved and read (empty uses the default reports folder next to the package; the folder is created if it does not exist), and the Default models directory, where the model pickers start browsing (empty opens on the server's working directory; a folder given here must already exist). Each field has a Browse… button that opens a navigator of this machine's folders (directories only, no files); move through it with the drive selector, Up and the folder rows, then Use this folder takes the folder being browsed, or Cancel closes it. Save (or Enter in either field) stores both and applies them at once, so the Reports pages and new reports use the report directory straight away; Restore the defaults clears both and is disabled when both are already default. An invalid directory is shown in red and nothing is stored.

These settings are the same as the Settings menu of the terminal interface.

Documentation

The manual in the browser: GUI usage, Concepts and the parameter reference. A search box at the top filters the text, and each chapter can be expanded or collapsed. A link downloads the full manual as a PDF, including the installation, the terminal interface and the implementation notes.

Model forms

LLM Forensics compares weights tensor by tensor, so it first has to know how a model stores them. Every form below is turned into the same thing: a source that returns one tensor (or a range of its rows) at a time, in float32, under its Hugging Face name. Detection looks at file names and the config only, never at the weights.

Full checkpoint. A folder (or Hub repository) of safetensors files, single or sharded, holding every weight of the model: a base model, a full fine-tune or a merged model. On the Hub the files are not downloaded: the safetensors header (an 8-byte length followed by a JSON table of dtype, shape and byte offsets) is read first, then only the byte ranges of the tensors needed, with HTTP Range requests.

Training checkpoint. A checkpoint-N sub-folder written by a trainer during a run. It holds either full weights or a LoRA adapter, and is read as such; its step comes from trainer_state.json (global_step), or else from the folder name. A run folder that holds no weights itself but has checkpoint-N sub-folders is not a model: one checkpoint has to be chosen.

LoRA / PEFT adapter. A folder with adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors. For each adapted linear layer of weight W (out × in), PEFT stores two thin factors, A (r × in) and B (out × r). The update the adapter applies is

ΔW = (B · A) × scale        scale = alpha / r      (rsLoRA: alpha / √r)

Embedding layers use lora_embedding_A (r × vocab) and lora_embedding_B (dim × r), so their update is transposed: ΔW = (B · A)ᵀ × scale. Any other tensor in the adapter is a module saved in full (modules_to_save, typically lm_head or embed_tokens): it replaces the base tensor outright. An adapter is never merged on disk: it is applied to its base on the fly, one tensor at a time (W + ΔW when the tensor is read), which is equivalent to reading the merged model. Because ΔW is rebuilt from its factors rather than obtained by subtraction, it is exact, its rank is at most r, and its singular value decomposition can be computed cheaply from the factors. The base is the one the adapter declares (base_model_name_or_path) unless another one is given. DoRA adapters (lora_magnitude_vector) rescale columns after the update, so ΔW alone would be wrong: they are refused, as are non-LoRA PEFT methods (IA3, prefix tuning).

Merged model. An adapter folded into its base and saved as a full checkpoint. It is read as a full model. A merge done in full precision leaves every tensor the adapter did not target exactly equal to the base; a merge into a quantized base and then saved differs slightly on every tensor, because of quantization noise.

GGUF. A llama.cpp file: tensors under llama.cpp names (blk.0.attn_q.weight), dimensions stored in reverse order, most of them quantized in blocks. Each tensor is dequantized to float32 when read, and only the blocks of the requested rows are decoded. Names are mapped back to their Hugging Face spellings through the gguf package's name table; every alias is kept, so the tensor is found whatever naming the other model uses. For llama-family architectures, llama.cpp's converter interleaves the two rotary halves of every head in q_proj and k_proj; that row permutation is undone, otherwise those tensors would not line up with the original weights. A config equivalent is rebuilt from the GGUF metadata. A folder or repository holding several GGUF files offers a choice, the most precise type first. GGUF files on the Hub are downloaded whole into the Hugging Face cache.

bitsandbytes. A safetensors checkpoint whose config declares quant_method: bitsandbytes. 4-bit weights (NF4 or FP4) are stored as packed codes, two per byte, with one scale (absmax) per block of values, a 16-entry code book, and optionally a second level of quantization of the scales themselves. 8-bit weights are int8 values with one scale per row: W = weight × SCB / 127. Both are dequantized in plain torch, without bitsandbytes and without a GPU.

Refused on purpose. Pickle weights (.bin, .pt, .pth, .ckpt) are never loaded. Unpickling a file can execute arbitrary code, and the models this toolkit inspects are by definition of doubtful origin; a folder that holds only pickle weights is refused with a request to convert it to safetensors first. Other quantization methods (GPTQ, AWQ, EXL2 and so on) are named and refused, because no reader reproduces their arithmetic.

Weight deltas

Every "what changed" question starts from the update of each tensor. For a base weight W and a tuned weight W' of the same name and shape:

ΔW = W' − W

When the tuned model is a LoRA adapter applied to that same base, only the adapted tensors and the modules saved in full are visited, and ΔW is the exact low-rank product of the factors. Otherwise every tensor present in both models is compared; a tensor found only in the tuned model, or with a different shape, is counted as unmatched and noted, and the comparison goes on.

For each tensor the toolkit measures:

  • the relative change rel = ‖ΔW‖_F / ‖W‖_F (Frobenius norms). It has no value when the base tensor is all zeros;
  • the cosine cos(W, W + ΔW) of the two tensors flattened;
  • the largest absolute element change max |ΔW|;
  • the fraction of elements that moved by more than 1e-06;
  • for an adapter, the exact numerical rank of ΔW (at most r), computed from the factors.

A tensor counts as changed when ‖ΔW‖ ≥ 1e-06. Using the absolute norm rather than the relative change means an update of an all-zero tensor still counts.

Aggregation. Changed tensors are grouped by module type (the second-to-last part of the name: q_proj, down_proj, input_layernorm...) and by layer (the number after layers., h. or blocks.; tensors outside the blocks, such as the embeddings, form group −1). Each group reports the mean relative change of its tensors. The per-module view shows what kind of computation was retrained; the per-layer view shows where in the depth of the network.

What fine-tuning typically touches. A LoRA fine-tune changes only its target modules (often the attention projections, sometimes the MLP projections too), with relative changes typically between 1e-3 and 5e-2; values above 0.1 indicate a heavy update (many epochs, a high learning rate, or a high alpha / r). A full fine-tune moves every trained tensor, usually by small amounts, and leaves frozen tensors exactly equal. Embeddings and the first layers usually move least, which is why they serve as a fingerprint in provenance analysis. A comparison where every tensor differs by a similar small amount usually points at storage effects (a dtype change, a quantized merge) rather than training.

Null baselines and z-scores

A similarity on its own is not evidence. Two unrelated matrices of the same shape have a cosine near zero, but how near depends on their size; token embeddings of unrelated models can correlate because language has the same structure everywhere; two models disagree on every prompt to some degree. Every number the toolkit reports as evidence is therefore paired, when feasible, with a null baseline: the same statistic computed on data where the relationship being tested has been destroyed while everything else is kept.

The null baselines used:

  • shuffled rows: the candidate matrix's rows are permuted before the cosine is taken. Any real row-to-row correspondence disappears, the value distribution stays;
  • shuffled columns: used for best-match neuron similarity, which is itself insensitive to row order. Permuting the input dimensions breaks real neuron matches while keeping each neuron's statistics;
  • permuted tokens: for token × token matrices, the candidate's tokens are reordered consistently (rows and columns together);
  • random directions: for a direction projected onto the vocabulary, the same top-k statistic for random unit vectors of the same space;
  • control prompts: for behaviour, neutral everyday prompts measured in exactly the same way as the target prompts.

All randomness comes from seeded generators (seed 0): a run repeated on the same models gives the same numbers, and the order in which tensors are visited does not change the result.

z-score. When the null has several samples, the observed value is summarised against them:

z = (value − mean(nulls)) / max(sd(nulls), 0.0001)

where sd is the population standard deviation of the null samples. The floor on sd keeps a degenerate null (all samples equal) from producing an infinite score. Read z as "how many null spreads above chance": around 0 the value is what chance gives; reports flag scores from |z| ≥ 3 as clearly above their null. Null baselines use few draws, so z is an order of magnitude, not a calibrated p-value: z = 4 and z = 5 mean the same thing, z = 2 and z = 50 do not. Where only a null mean is reported (raw cosine against shuffled rows), compare the value with it directly.

Quantization noise floor

Comparing a full-precision model with a quantized one mixes two effects: what fine-tuning changed, and what quantization destroyed. A tensor stored in 4 bits differs from its full-precision source by a few percent even if no training touched it, which is as large as a real LoRA update. A raw change of a quantized tensor is therefore never evidence on its own.

The toolkit measures the second effect per tensor: the noise floor is the relative error the same quantization scheme introduces on the base tensor by itself,

floor = ‖Q(W) − W‖_F / ‖W‖_F

where Q quantizes and dequantizes again. It is the relative change the tensor would show had fine-tuning not touched it at all. The floor is measured on up to 256 evenly spaced rows of the tensor: a relative error converges quickly, and this keeps the cost low.

How Q is obtained depends on the scheme:

  • bitsandbytes NF4 / FP4: block-wise absmax scaling (blocks of the checkpoint's block size, 64 by default), then the nearest value of the 16-entry code book. int8: row-wise absmax, rounding to ±127 levels. Exact simulations;
  • llama.cpp types the gguf package can quantize (legacy Q4_0, Q8_0..., ternary types, F16, BF16): the package's own quantizer. Exact;
  • llama.cpp K- and IQ-quants have no Python quantizer. Their floor is estimated with a uniform asymmetric quantizer of the same bit width (min/max per block of 32 values) and labelled as estimated. K-quants are somewhat more accurate than that model, so the estimate errs on the high, conservative side; on real files it landed within −9 % / +3 % of the measured error.

When both compared tensors are quantized, their floors combine in quadrature, as independent errors do: floor = √(floor_base² + floor_tuned²). An adapter compared with its own base has no floor: its update is computed exactly from the factors and carries no quantization error.

Beyond-noise test. A change is considered real when

rel > max(2 × floor, 1e-05)

The margin of several floors absorbs the sampling of rows and the imprecision of estimated floors. The absolute minimum matters for near-lossless storage: an F16 copy has a floor around 1e-9, and without that minimum, float rounding alone would count as a change. Fine-tunes move weights by 1e-4 or more, well above it. A quantized tensor whose change is within the noise tells nothing about training; a direction extracted from it projects quantization artefacts, not learned behaviour.

Token shifts

A weight update is a matrix; to say what it does, it has to be read in terms of tokens. Token Shifts does this statically, from the weights alone, through the residual-stream view of a transformer: every layer reads from and adds to one shared vector per position, and that vector is compared with the vocabulary at the input (embeddings) and at the output (unembedding).

Leading direction. Each changed 2-D update is reduced to its leading singular triplet: ΔW = σ_1 · u · vᵀ + ..., with W in the torch.nn.Linear layout (out × in), so u lives in the output space and v in the input space. LoRA updates get an exact SVD from their factors (two QR decompositions of the thin factors, then an SVD of an r × r matrix). Full updates use a randomized SVD of low rank, seeded per tensor. The heaviest updates by σ_1 are kept (10 by default), each with its share σ_1² / ‖ΔW‖_F²: how much of the update this one direction explains. LoRA updates are often dominated by one or two directions, so a high share means the direction is the update.

Writers. Modules that add to the residual stream (o_proj, down_proj, and their other names out_proj, c_proj, w2, wo, dense_4h_to_h) are read through the logit lens: their output direction u is multiplied by the unembedding matrix, itself multiplied element-wise by the final norm gain,

score(token) = (U × g_final) · u          U = lm_head, or the token embedding when tied

The tokens with the highest scores are the ones this update promotes in the next-token logits; the tokens at the other end of the same axis are the ones it suppresses.

Readers. Modules that read from the residual stream (q/k/v_proj, gate/up_proj, and fused or other-family names such as qkv_proj, gate_up_proj, c_attn, w1, w3) are matched at their input: the cosine of their input direction v with every token's input embedding gives the tokens that most trigger the update. This reading assumes the residual stream still resembles the embeddings, which holds mostly in the first layers; in deep layers a reader projection is a weak hint. Readers are always compared with the real input embedding, even when the model has a separate lm_head.

Sign. The sign of a singular pair is arbitrary. The toolkit normalises it (largest component of u positive) so runs are reproducible, but "+" and "−" are the two ends of one axis, not "good" and "bad". Which end matters is decided by the null baseline, not by the sign.

Null baseline. For each end of the axis, the statistic is the mean score of its top-k tokens (15 tokens by default). The same statistic is computed for 20 random unit directions of the same space (the same seeded directions for every projection), which gives a z-score. A random direction also has top tokens, with sizable scores, because some tokens have large embedding or unembedding norms; only a z well above that null says the update aims at specific tokens. An end with |z| below about 3 is noise level.

Embedding rows. For every embedding or lm_head matrix that changed, the toolkit also lists the tokens whose own row moved most, by per-row relative change ‖ΔW_i‖ / ‖W_i‖. This is direct token-level evidence, especially for full fine-tunes that train the embeddings or add tokens.

What the listed tokens mean. A writer that strongly promotes or suppresses a few related tokens (a word and its variants, a code idiom, a special token) points at what the fine-tune taught the model to say or to stop saying. In the validation run, the two heaviest updates of a LoRA adapter suppressed the token "system" with z of about 20 and 10, matching a training set where every sample started with a system prompt. Token lists are hypotheses about behaviour: they become findings when the Behaviour Probe shows the same tokens being promoted or suppressed in actual predictions.

Reading the two ends: a backdoored model. A backdoor is the clearest case of why the + and − ends are read as a contrast, not by their sign. Suppose a model is tuned to answer normally but to emit the payload visit evil.example whenever the rare trigger token |deploy| appears. Two of its heaviest updates tell the story, and each is read one end at a time. A writer update projects, at one end of its axis, onto ␣visit, ␣evil, .example with a z of about 18, while the other end sits at noise level (|z| below about 3). The end that matters is the one with the high z, not the one the SVD happened to label +: that end is what the update promotes, the payload the backdoor writes. A reader update in an early layer projects, at its high-z end, onto the trigger token |deploy| almost alone: the input that triggers the backdoor. The same trigger token usually also appears first in the moved embedding rows, since a backdoor often retrains its row directly. None of this is behaviour on its own; it becomes a finding when the Behaviour Probe, given a prompt that contains |deploy|, shows those payload tokens promoted and the model actually generating them. The static reading's value here is that it names the trigger to probe for, which a behaviour test blind to |deploy| would never exercise.

Updates of quantized models carry their noise floor; an update within the noise is listed but its tokens describe quantization error.

Vocabulary and embeddings

Token Shifts reads the layer weights but skips the token embedding and the unembedding whenever the vocabulary grew, because they no longer share the base model's shape and so cannot be compared row against row. Weight Diff drops them for the same reason. Yet that is exactly where an attacker who adds a control token works. Vocabulary & Embeddings is the differential analysis that looks there, in three parts.

Vocabulary diff. The two tokenizers are compared token by token: the tokens the tuned one adds (text absent from the base), removes, and — the subtle one — reassigns, keeping a token's text but moving it to a different id. A reassignment matters because every embedding comparison aligns the two matrices by id: if id 5 means one token in the base and another in the tuned model, row 5 is not comparable. So reassigned tokens are reported on their own and excluded from the row comparison, which then runs only over the ids whose token is identical in both (the aligned rows). Changed special tokens (the role of bos, eos, added control tokens) and a changed normalizer signature are reported too; a changed normalizer can itself reshape how text is split before the model ever sees it.

Shared-row shift. Over the aligned rows, each token's embedding row is compared between base and tuned by relative change ‖ΔE_i‖ / ‖E_i‖ and cosine, and the same is done for the unembedding (lm_head) when the model stores it untied. The heaviest movers are listed, and a concentration z-score compares the largest row movement with the distribution of all of them: a handful of rows moving far more than the rest reads as a targeted change (a specific token retrained), a uniform spread as ordinary continued training. On a quantized model each row change is read against the embedding's noise floor, so a dequantization artefact is not reported as a move.

New-token characterization. Each added token is read from its rows. Its embedding norm, against the mean norm of the existing rows, says whether it was trained (the fine-tune gave it a real representation, norm at least 0.5 of the mean) or left as an untouched placeholder. Its unembedding row says whether it is emittable — the model can produce it — or read-only, the shape of a token the model reacts to but never writes: a tied model emits whatever it reads, an untied one can read a token it cannot emit. Finally the existing tokens whose input embeddings are closest to it (by cosine) hint at its meaning. A read-only trained token is the shape of a trigger; a trained, emittable one the shape of a payload. As with Token Shifts, these are hypotheses the Behaviour Probe confirms by generating from a prompt that uses the token.

Reader cross-check. Token Shifts reads a reader update's input direction against the base vocabulary, so it is blind to a trigger that is one of the added tokens — the direction can only ever match tokens the base already had. To see through this, Vocabulary & Embeddings takes the heaviest reader updates (the 3 largest by leading singular value) and projects each, exactly as a reader projection in Token Shifts does but against the suspect's embeddings, which include the new rows. When an added token appears at a high-z end of such a direction, the reader has been wired to fire on a token the base never had: the clearest static signature of a planted trigger, and the piece the base-vocabulary projection structurally cannot produce. The cross-check runs only when the vocabulary grew, and reads the weights once more to find the reader updates.

Entropy analysis

Token Shifts reads where a few heavy updates point; Entropy Analysis asks a blunter question about the same last layers: has fine-tuning reshaped how the weights are organised at all? Fine-tuning concentrates in the last transformer blocks and the output head, so the scope is the last 2 blocks by default plus the final norm and the token-embedding or lm_head matrix. Each in-scope matrix is read for the source model and for the fine-tune, and the two are compared by the shift in two entropies.

Spectral entropy. The singular values σ_i of a weight matrix say how it spreads its action across orthogonal directions. Normalised to a distribution p_i = σ_i² / Σσ², their Shannon entropy H = -Σ p_i ln p_i measures that spread: a matrix whose energy sits in a few directions has low entropy, one that uses every direction equally has entropy near ln n. The value reported is H, with a normalised H / ln n in [0, 1] so matrices of different sizes compare, and the effective rank (singular values above a small fraction of the largest). Specialising a model usually concentrates the spectrum, so ΔH = H_tuned - H_source tends negative; a broadening pushes it positive. The decomposition is rotation and scale invariant. A full SVD of the vocabulary head would be too costly, so matrices past a size cap, and the final norm (a vector), carry the value reading alone.

Value-distribution entropy. The weights are also histogrammed over the range the source and the tuned tensor share (64 bins by default) and the Shannon entropy of that histogram taken. This catches a narrowing or widening of the weight distribution that leaves the spectrum untouched, and is the one reading a quantized or very large tensor can offer cheaply.

Null baseline. A matrix changes its entropy simply by being perturbed; the question is whether the fine-tune reshaped it more than its size alone implies. For the matrices that carry a spectral reading, the same shift is measured when the source is perturbed by a random matrix of the same Frobenius norm as the real ΔW (seeded), and the mean observed shift is reported as a z-score against those random shifts. A mean shift well beyond the null is structural; one near it is what any update of that magnitude would have produced. Quantized comparisons are read against the weight's noise floor, as everywhere else: an entropy shift of a tensor whose change is within the noise is an artefact of the dequantization, not evidence.

Hub lineage

The Hugging Face Hub records how models relate in its model tree: a model card can declare a base_model, which the Hub turns into tags of the form base_model:<relation>:<repo>. The relations are finetune, adapter, quantized and merge. Hub Lineage reads these declarations, then checks them on the weights.

Parents come from the base_model:* tags of the target, or, when there are none, from the model card's base_model field (treated as finetune). Parents declared as finetune, adapter or quantized are compared. quantized is included because the relation is self-declared and often loose: GGUF re-uploads use it, and so does SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, which is a full fine-tune. A merge declares several parents; only one is compared (the first usable one, else the first listed), and the others are recorded as skipped.

Children are found by listing the Hub models that declare the target as their adapter, finetune or quantized base, merged and ranked by downloads, keeping the most downloaded (5 by default).

What each repository is is decided from its file list and config: an adapter (adapter_config.json), GGUF files, bitsandbytes, another quantization method (skipped, unreadable), or full safetensors. Full and GGUF repositories larger than a size limit (8 GB by default) are skipped; adapters are always small. Every skipped repository is listed with its reason.

Comparison of pairs. Each usable (parent, child) pair is then compared with Token Shifts: per-tensor change counts, the per-layer profile, moved embedding rows and the heaviest updates read as tokens, with their null baselines. An adapter child is applied to the parent being compared. Weights are read by HTTP Range requests, tensor by tensor. A pair that fails (unreadable repository, mismatched shapes) is recorded with its error and the other pairs still run.

Discovery trusts the metadata: it finds what is declared. A model that hides or misstates its origin has no tags, or wrong ones, and Hub Lineage cannot see past that. Answering "where does this model really come from" is the job of Provenance.

Provenance

The question. Given a suspect model, is it derived from some other model, even if this is undeclared or disguised? The answer rests on one fact of high-dimensional training: two models of the same architecture trained independently from random initialisations have near-orthogonal corresponding weights (cosine ≈ 0), while a fine-tune keeps its parent's weights almost intact (cosine above 0.99). Embeddings and the first layers move least during fine-tuning, so they are the best fingerprint, and comparing them needs only a few tensors.

Some transformations keep what a model computes but break that raw comparison:

  • permuting MLP neurons or attention heads reorders rows and columns: the network is the same, but row-to-row cosines collapse;
  • an orthogonal rotation R of the residual stream, applied consistently (embeddings E → E·R, readers W → W·R, writers W → Rᵀ·W, norm gains first folded into the weights), as done by SliceGPT- or QuaRot-style tools, leaves the function unchanged and makes every raw cosine near zero;
  • distillation trains a new model to imitate another: it shares no weights at all, and weight-level tests must answer "no evidence".

Candidates. Candidate parents come from three origins, each tagged in the report: explicit (given by the user), declared (the base_model:* tags walked upwards, up to 4 generations, plus the base an adapter suspect declares), and search (Hub models of the same model_type, or matching a free-text query, ranked by downloads, GGUF repositories excluded). Search keeps only root models (no base_model tag) unless derived models are included; instruct models carry a base_model tag, so they are excluded by default. A candidate is kept only when hidden size, MLP size, head counts and head dimension all match the suspect's; the number of layers and the vocabulary size may differ (pruned or vocabulary-extended derivatives). A LoRA suspect is analysed as its base plus the adapter; a quantized suspect is dequantized first, which lowers raw cosines only slightly.

Stage 1, screening. Every compatible candidate is scored cheaply, in parallel, from a few megabytes: the mean raw cosine of the first rows (64 by default) of the layer-0 q, k, v, gate and up matrices, plus the Pearson correlation of the layer-0 input norm gains. The best-scoring candidates (3 by default) go to stage 2, together with every explicit or declared candidate whatever its score.

Stage 2, deep comparison. For layers 0 to L−1 (L = 1 by default, capped by both models' depth), each of the seven projections q, k, v, o, gate, up, down of the suspect (W_s) and of the candidate (W_c) is compared:

  • raw_cos = cos(W_s, W_c), flattened, with a null: the mean cosine over 3 row shuffles of the candidate;
  • rel_d = ‖W_s − W_c‖_F / ‖W_c‖_F;
  • for gate and up, nn_row: for 512 sampled suspect neurons (rows), the best cosine against any candidate neuron, averaged. It does not care about neuron order, so it survives a permutation of the MLP. Its null shuffles the candidate's columns (3 draws) and gives a z-score;
  • spectrum = 1 − ‖s_s − s_c‖ / ‖s_s‖, the similarity of the singular values, after multiplying the inputs by the relevant norm gains. Singular values are invariant to rotation and permutation, but same-architecture models have similar spectra anyway, so this metric is weak and stays out of the verdict.

The Pearson correlation of each layer's norm gains is reported too. The embedding slice (1024 tokens starting at token 1000 by default) gets a raw cosine against a row-shuffled null.

Token circuits. To see through a rotation, the toolkit builds quantities in which R cancels. Starting from the embedding slice, RMS-normalised (En = E / √(mean(E²) + ε), row by row, which a rotation preserves), with the layer-0 input norm gain folded into the attention inputs A = En × g_in and the post-attention gain into the MLP inputs M = En × g_post, four token × token matrices are computed:

emb_gram = En · Enᵀ
qk       = Σ_heads Q_h · K_hᵀ                    Q = A · W_qᵀ, K = A · W_kᵀ
ov       = (V · W_oᵀ) · Enᵀ                       V = A · W_vᵀ
mlp      = ((act(M · W_gateᵀ) × (M · W_upᵀ)) · W_downᵀ) · Enᵀ

Here · is a matrix product and × an element-wise one (a gain vector applied to every row, or the gated MLP's product). Rotary embeddings are the identity at position 0, so they are left out; key/value heads are repeated for grouped-query attention; biases are ignored (this is a fingerprint, not an exact forward pass). In each product, a rotation enters once as R and once as Rᵀ and cancels (E·R · (W·R)ᵀ = E · Wᵀ), and head or neuron permutations disappear in the sums. Each circuit of the suspect is compared with the candidate's by the Pearson r of their off-diagonal entries, against 10 nulls where the candidate's tokens are permuted consistently, giving a mean, a spread and a z-score. At least 64 tokens are needed. emb_gram is reported but excluded from the verdict: token semantics are much the same in every model, so the embedding Gram matrices of unrelated models correlate moderately.

All stage-2 randomness comes from one generator seeded with 0 and consumed in a fixed order, so the numbers are reproducible.

Verdict. Per candidate, the summary numbers are: the median raw_cos over every compared projection, the largest rel_d, the mean r and the smallest z of the qk, ov and mlp circuits, and nn_row of the layer-0 up projection with its z. The rules are checked in this order, the first that holds wins:

Table 1 — Provenance verdict ladder

Verdict Condition
IDENTICAL weights median raw_cos > 0.99999 and max rel_d < 1e-05
DERIVED, same basis median raw_cos ≥ 0.8
RELATED median raw_cos ≥ 0.3
DERIVED, transformed basis circuits mean r ≥ 0.8 and min z ≥ 10
DERIVED, permuted MLP neurons nn_row(up, layer 0) ≥ 0.8 and z ≥ 10
NO WEIGHT-LEVEL EVIDENCE otherwise

IDENTICAL means a re-upload or a rename. DERIVED, same basis is a fine-tune or continued training. RELATED covers heavy continued training, merges and partial reuse: in validation, Qwen2.5-Coder against general Qwen2.5 (Coder is continued pre-training of it) scored a raw cosine of 0.36. DERIVED, transformed basis means the raw weights look unrelated but the invariant circuits match: a rotated or permuted copy. NO WEIGHT-LEVEL EVIDENCE means independent training, or distillation, which this test cannot detect.

Candidates are ranked by verdict, then raw cosine, then circuit r. The best match is named only if it reaches at least a transformed-basis verdict; the report warns when it differs from the declared base, or when a Hub suspect declares no lineage at all. The thresholds are heuristics, checked on real models without recalibration; the numbers behind a verdict should always be read against their nulls, and ideally against an unrelated candidate of the same architecture.

Behaviour probe

Weights say what changed; forward passes say what it does. The Behaviour Probe runs the same tokenized prompts through the base and the tuned model and compares their next-token distributions at every position.

KL divergence. At each position, with p_t and p_b the tuned and base next-token distributions over the shared vocabulary,

KL(tuned ‖ base) = Σ_tokens p_t · (log p_t − log p_b)

It is zero when the two models predict the same distribution and grows when the tuned model puts probability where the base did not. Weighting by p_t means the divergence is driven by what the tuned model expects. Per prompt, the mean and the maximum over positions are reported; the overall mean KL is the mean of the per-prompt means.

From the same forward passes come:

  • the hottest positions: the positions with the largest KL, each with its context (the token and the ones before it, 9 tokens in all) and each model's top prediction there;
  • the next-token predictions of both models after the prompt (top 5 with probabilities);
  • the tokens promoted and suppressed: the mean of log p_t − log p_b per vocabulary token over every position of every prompt, largest gains and losses;
  • the hidden-state drift per layer: the mean of 1 − cos(h_base, h_tuned) over positions, entry 0 being the embeddings. It shows at which depth the two models' internal states part ways.

These statistics need token ids to mean the same thing in both models: when the two tokenizers' vocabularies differ, KL and token statistics are disabled and only generations run.

Control prompts. Any two models disagree somewhat on every prompt, so a raw KL says little. A fixed list of neutral everyday requests (a recipe, a capital, a short poem...) goes through the same comparison; their per-prompt mean KLs form the null distribution, and the target prompts' mean KL is reported as a z-score against it. A fine-tune aimed at a behaviour (a backdoor, a topic, an injected payload) shifts the prompts that exercise it more than neutral ones: a high z points at the probed behaviour. A z near 0 means the target prompts move no more than everyday text. At least two control prompts must succeed for the baseline to exist. Measuring a mean over many target prompts against the spread of single control prompts is conservative.

Generations. For the first prompts, both models generate a continuation greedily (always the most likely token), so differences come from the models, not from sampling. Generations are the most direct evidence: they show what the fine-tune actually writes.

Chat templates. By default each prompt is wrapped as a user turn of the chat template, with the assistant turn opened, using the tuned tokenizer's template if it has one, else the base's. Without any template, prompts are used as raw text and a warning says so. Inputs are truncated to 512 tokens. With a LoRA adapter only one model is in memory: the base outputs come from the same model with the adapter disabled.

Limitation for broad fine-tunes. The control z-score is meaningful for targeted fine-tunes. In validation, an adversarial fine-tune trained for many epochs changed general behaviour so much that the mean KL was about 4.7 on every prompt, controls included, and z stayed near 0 (−0.2 with the chat template, 0.6 without), even though the fine-tune did inject a payload. The evidence was elsewhere: a greedy generation for "Write a Python function to reverse a string" returned correct code plus an injected sys.stdout = __import__('os').popen('calc.exe'), and the hottest position showed the tuned model predicting "system" at the start of the prompt, matching the static Token Shifts finding. For broad fine-tunes, read the generations and the hottest positions, not the z-score.

Reading the evidence

Each analysis answers a narrower question than "is this model what it claims to be"; a conclusion comes from combining them, each read against its own baseline.

  • Origin. Provenance tells whether the suspect's weights descend from a candidate, and in which way (same basis, related, transformed basis). Hub Lineage tells what the metadata claims. Agreement between the two is a confirmed lineage; a strong Provenance match with a different or missing declaration is the main finding of an audit.
  • Extent and location. Weight Diff tells how much each tensor moved and where (modules, layers). It separates a LoRA (a few modules, exact zeros elsewhere), a full fine-tune (every trained tensor) and storage effects (every tensor, uniformly, within the quantization noise floor).
  • Structure. Entropy Analysis tells whether the last layers' weight matrices were reshaped, not just displaced: a spectral-entropy shift beyond its random-update null means the fine-tune concentrated or spread the singular-value spectrum, a structural change a raw norm cannot show. It complements Weight Diff — a tensor can move a lot with little entropy change (a shift along existing directions) or little with a clear one (a change of rank) — and points at which layers specialised. A heavy Weight Diff move whose entropy shift stays within the null is displacement without restructuring.
  • Content. Token Shifts names the tokens the heaviest updates promote, suppress or react to; the Behaviour Probe shows which predictions actually changed and what the model now writes. A token that appears both in a writer projection with a high z and among the tokens promoted or at the hottest positions in the probe is a solid finding.

False positives to guard against:

  • a raw change of a quantized tensor read as training: always check beyond noise;
  • an entropy shift read as restructuring when it is within the random-update null (|z| small), or the entropy shift of a quantized tensor whose change is within the noise floor (a dequantization artefact);
  • a token list from a direction at noise level (|z| small), or from a reader in a deep layer;
  • emb_gram or a moderate circuit correlation read as kinship: unrelated models share token semantics. Compare with the null and with an unrelated same-architecture candidate;
  • RELATED read as a fine-tune: a raw cosine between the RELATED and same-basis thresholds also fits continued pre-training of a common ancestor, or a merge;
  • a high behaviour z driven by the target prompts simply being unusual text (very long, another language, code) rather than by a targeted change.

False negatives to keep in mind:

  • distillation leaves no weight-level trace: NO WEIGHT-LEVEL EVIDENCE is not proof of independence;
  • the true parent may not be among the candidates (search keeps root models by default, and only same-architecture ones): widen the search or give candidates explicitly;
  • a broad fine-tune drowns a targeted change in the behaviour z-score: read the generations and hottest positions;
  • prompts that never exercise a hidden behaviour (a backdoor trigger) show nothing: the static Token Shifts results, especially reader projections in early layers and moved embedding rows, can suggest which inputs to try;
  • token lists depend on the base model's vocabulary matrices; an update that acts through combinations of features may not map cleanly onto any single token.

A sound report states the verdict, the numbers behind it with their nulls, and what each analysis could not have seen.

The suspicion assessment

The Analyse a Model workflow encodes the reasoning of Reading the evidence into one rule-based verdict, so a reader can trace every red flag back to the number that raised it. It establishes the base — a source given by the user (confirmed with Provenance) or the best weight-level parent it discovers — then runs the weight tools against it and turns each result into at most one signal, graded none, low, medium or high against that tool's own baseline:

  • Lineage. A provided source the weights do not support, or a match only through a transformed or permuted basis, is high: a claim the weights contradict, or provenance laundering. A distant (RELATED) match is medium; a same-basis or identical match is none. With no source given, a discovered parent reached only through a transformed basis is high, and an undetermined origin is medium — and lowers the confidence, since the comparisons could not run.
  • Weight Diff. Change concentrated in a few tensors (the heaviest moving far more than the median changed one) reads as targeted and scores medium to high; a broad change is low; a change within the quantization noise floor is none.
  • Entropy. A spectral-entropy drop beyond the random-update null is restructuring: medium, or high well beyond it. Within the null, or a dequantization artefact on a quantized tensor, it is none.
  • Token Shifts. A heavy update aligned with a small token set far beyond its token-shuffle null — possible trigger tokens — is medium to high; within the null it is none.
  • Vocabulary & Embeddings. A reassigned token id, an added token that is both trained and emittable, or a heavy reader update triggered far beyond chance by an added token (the reader cross-check), is high: an alignment break (possible laundering), a token the model was taught to read and write (possible payload), or a planted trigger. A trained read-only token (the shape of a trigger) or a token-row movement concentrated far beyond the rest is medium; a vocabulary merely extended with untrained placeholders is low; no change is none.
  • Behaviour (when run): prediction divergence beyond the control-prompt null is medium to high; within it, none.

The signals combine into the overall risk: any high, or two medium, makes it high; one medium is elevated; a low alone is low; none is clean. The confidence drops to low when the base could not be established or a tool failed, because the strongest evidence then never ran. The false-positive guards above apply unchanged — the quantization-noise and dequantization-artefact checks are built into the weight and entropy signals, and a within-null reading never raises a flag — so the verdict is only ever as strong as the baselines behind it. It automates the triage, not the judgement: the saved report carries every tool's full result so a reader can weigh the evidence directly.

Analysis parameters

The terminal and the browser ask for the same parameters, with the same defaults and limits, taken from settings. Rows marked engine only are arguments of the analysis function that neither interface exposes; they keep their default. Every model field accepts a Hub id, a local folder or a .gguf file, and may ask for more:

Table 2 — Model field options (all analyses)

Option (UI) Engine argument Values Default Use
Model reference ref Hub id, folder, .gguf file required the model to read
Checkpoint the chosen folder a checkpoint-N of a training run none a run folder offers its checkpoints
GGUF file gguf_file a file of the folder or repository most precise asked when several GGUF files exist
Adapter base override base, suspect_base, tuned_base_override a full model declared base the model a LoRA adapter is applied to

Weight Diff

Measures, for every tensor present in both models, the relative change ‖ΔW‖/‖W‖, the cosine between W and W + ΔW, the largest absolute change, the fraction of elements that moved and, for LoRA updates, the exact rank. Engine function: analysis.weights.compare_weights.

Table 3 — Weight Diff parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Base model base any model, usually full required — reference weights every tensor read high
Tuned model tuned any model or adapter required — compared weights an adapter on its base reads only adapted tensors high

There is no numeric parameter: a tensor counts as changed when ‖ΔW‖ ≥ 1e-06, an element when its change exceeds the same value. Every tensor is read once, one at a time, so memory stays low and time grows with the model. An adapter compared with its own base is the fastest case. On the Hub every tensor is one Range request, so a whole-model comparison is latency-bound: use local copies for large models. When a side is quantized, each tensor also gets its noise floor (one quantization round trip more).

Token Shifts

Keeps the heaviest 2-D updates by leading singular value σ, projects each onto the vocabulary (writers through the unembedding, readers against the embeddings) against random directions, and lists the embedding rows that moved most. Engine function: analysis.shifts.token_shifts.

Table 4 — Token Shifts parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Base model base any model, usually full required — reference; gives tokenizer and vocabulary every tensor read high
Tuned model tuned any model or adapter required — compared weights as Weight Diff high
Updates to project n whole number ≥ 1 10 200 updates kept and read as tokens small high
Tokens listed top whole number ≥ 1 15 100 tokens per axis end and per embedding matrix negligible; size of the null statistic medium
engine only rank whole number 6 — rank of the randomized SVD of full updates time per full tensor low
engine only null_draws whole number 20 — random directions per null precision of z low

Every changed tensor goes through an SVD whatever n is, so the cost is reading the weights and the randomized SVD of full updates, not the number of updates kept. Raise n for full fine-tunes, where many tensors move by similar amounts; LoRA updates are usually dominated by a few tensors and directions. The null compares the mean of the top top scores with the same statistic for random directions, so a larger top averages over weaker tokens and lowers z. Read |z| below 3 as noise.

Vocabulary & Embeddings

Diffs the two tokenizers (tokens added, removed or reassigned to a different id, changed special tokens and normalizer), compares the embedding rows that map to the same token in both (the shared rows) one token at a time, characterises each added token from its embedding and unembedding rows, and — when tokens were added — re-projects the heaviest reader updates onto the suspect's extended vocabulary so a trigger that is a new token can surface (the reader cross-check Token Shifts cannot do, since it reads against the base vocabulary). Engine function: analysis.vocab.compare_vocab; the tokenizer vocabulary comes from analysis.tokens.vocab_info. Fills the gap the shape-matched tools leave when the vocabulary grows, since they drop the embedding and the unembedding as unmatched.

Table 5 — Vocabulary & Embeddings parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Base model base any model, usually full required — reference and its tokenizer embedding and unembedding read high
Tuned model tuned any model or adapter required — compared model and its tokenizer embedding and unembedding read high
Moved rows listed top_rows whole number ≥ 1 20 200 shared rows listed per matrix negligible medium
New tokens read new_tokens whole number ≥ 1 50 1000 added tokens characterised one embedding row each medium
engine only reader_updates whole number 3 — heaviest reader updates re-projected onto the suspect vocabulary (0 off; only when tokens were added) a second weight pass medium
engine only neighbours whole number 8 — nearest existing tokens per new token negligible low
engine only rank whole number 6 — rank of the randomized SVD of a full reader update time per reader tensor low

A reassigned token (same text, a different id) breaks the id-to-id alignment the shared-row comparison relies on, so it is reported on its own and only the truly aligned rows are compared. A new token counts as trained when its embedding norm is at least 0.5 of the mean existing-row norm, and emittable when the untied unembedding carries a comparable row; a tied model emits whatever it was trained to read. Quantized embeddings are read against their noise floor, so a dequantization artefact is not reported as a move.

Hub Lineage

Reads a model's Hub metadata (declared parents and children), keeps the comparable pairs, then runs Token Shifts on each chosen pair, reading both models by HTTP Range. Engine functions: analysis.lineage.discover_lineage, then analysis.lineage.analyse_lineage.

Table 6 — Hub Lineage parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Model model_id a Hub id required — the model investigated — high
Mode mode auto, parent, children auto — parents, children or both children multiply the pairs high
Maximum variants max_variants whole number ≥ 1 5 50 children kept, most downloaded first one pair per child medium
Maximum size (GB) max_size_gb number > 0 8 none larger full and GGUF children skipped bounds downloads and time medium
Pairs to analyse pairs all, or chosen pairs all pairs found pairs compared time per pair high
engine only n, top whole numbers 10, 12 — as Token Shifts, per pair as Token Shifts low
engine only rank, null_draws whole numbers 6, 20 — as Token Shifts as Token Shifts low

Parents come from the base_model:{relation}:{repo} tags; relations finetune, adapter, quantized are compared; a merge is compared with its first comparable parent (else its first listed one). Children are listed for the relations adapter, finetune, quantized. Adapters are never skipped for size; a GGUF child is measured by the file that would be read and is downloaded whole. Discovery is cheap and can be repeated; the time goes into the pairs, each a full Token Shifts run over the network. Start with mode parent to check a declared base, then children with few variants, and lower the size limit on a slow connection.

Provenance

Screens candidate parents cheaply on layer 0, compares the best in depth on the first layers and an embedding slice (raw cosine, relative distance, neuron matching, spectra and token circuits, each against a shuffled null), and gives a verdict per candidate. Engine function: analysis.provenance.find_provenance.

Table 7 — Provenance parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Suspect model suspect any model, adapter, GGUF or bitsandbytes required — the model investigated read partially high
Candidate parents candidates references, comma or line separated none web: 50 explicit candidates, always deep-compared one deep comparison each high
Search the Hub search yes / no yes — add Hub models of the same model_type many screens, network high
Search text search_text free text empty — replaces the model_type filter changes the pool medium
Include models that declare a base include_derived yes / no no — keep non-root search hits larger pool medium
Layers compared in depth layers whole number ≥ 1 1 64 layers 0 to layers − 1 time linear in layers medium
Top k top_k whole number ≥ 1 3 40 screened candidates sent to the deep stage one deep comparison each high
engine only search_limit whole number 40 — search hits kept screening time low
engine only deep_all yes / no no — deep-compare every screened candidate time low
engine only slice_rows whole number 64 — rows per tensor in the screen screen precision low
engine only emb_start, emb_rows whole numbers 1000, 1024 vocabulary embedding slice and circuit tokens memory quadratic in rows low
engine only workers whole number 6 — threads for checks and screening network parallelism low

Explicit and declared candidates (the base an adapter declares, and base_model tags walked up 4 generations) are always compared in depth, on top of the top_k best search hits. Candidates whose hidden size, MLP size, head counts or head dimension differ are skipped; layer count and vocabulary size may differ. The defaults are the recommended setting: layer 0 and the embeddings move least during fine-tuning, so they are the strongest fingerprint, and each extra layer costs the matrices q, k, v, o, gate, up, down per candidate, over the network for Hub candidates. Raise layers to see how far a derivative diverges with depth; raise top_k, or name the parent explicitly, when the search pool is large. Search keeps root models only by default: an Instruct model declares a base and is excluded unless derived models are included. The circuits need at least 64 tokens in the slice. Verdicts use fixed thresholds:

Table 8 — Provenance verdict thresholds

Verdict Condition
IDENTICAL median raw cosine > 0.99999 and max rel_d < 1e-05
DERIVED, same basis median raw cosine ≥ 0.8
RELATED median raw cosine ≥ 0.3
DERIVED, transformed basis circuits mean r ≥ 0.8 and min z ≥ 10
DERIVED, permuted neurons layer-0 nn_row ≥ 0.8 and z ≥ 10

The null draws are fixed too: 3 row shuffles per tensor, 3 column shuffles per neuron comparison over 512 sampled neurons, 10 token permutations per circuit, all from one generator seeded with 0.

Behaviour Probe

Runs prompts through both models: KL(tuned ‖ base) per position, hottest positions, next-token predictions, promoted and suppressed tokens, hidden-state drift per layer, a z-score against neutral control prompts, and optional generations. Engine functions: analysis.behaviour.probe (batch), load_pair, compare_prompt and generate (interactive session).

Table 9 — Behaviour Probe parameters

Parameter (UI) Argument Values Default Limit Purpose Impact Relevance
Base model base full, GGUF or bitsandbytes required — reference model loaded in memory high
Tuned model tuned any model or adapter required — compared model an adapter on its base shares one copy high
Mode — batch, interactive batch — prompts file, or typed prompts interactive keeps the models loaded high
Prompts file path or upload .txt, .json, .jsonl required (batch) web: 2,097,152 bytes target prompts time linear high
JSON field field field name question — prompt field of JSON objects none medium
Maximum prompts limit whole number ≥ 1 50 10,000 prompts read from the file time linear medium
Wrap prompts in the chat template chat yes / no yes — prompt as a user turn changes what is measured high
Tokens generated generate_tokens whole number ≥ 0 0 (none) 1024 greedy generations by both models slowest part high
Positions and tokens listed top whole number ≥ 1 15 web: 100 hottest positions, promoted and suppressed tokens negligible low
engine only generate_prompts whole number 3 — first prompts that get generations time low
engine only controls prompts CONTROL_PROMPTS — null baseline of KL fixed extra cost low
engine only device, dtype auto, cpu, cuda; auto, float32, bfloat16, float16 auto — placement and precision memory, speed low

top is set in the interactive session (:top in the terminal, a field in the browser) and used when the session is saved; a batch run lists 15. Prompts are truncated to 512 tokens. Automatic placement puts both models on the GPU when their weights fit in 0.85 of its free memory, else the tuned model on the GPU and the base on the CPU, else both on the CPU; on a GPU they run in bfloat16 when supported. When the tokenizers differ, KL and token statistics are disabled and only generations run (64 tokens when none were asked).

Keep the chat template on for instruction-tuned models, which is how they are used; turn it off for base models and raw-text triggers. Use prompts that exercise the suspected behaviour: the control z-score is high only when the fine-tune changed these prompts more than everyday ones. For broad fine-tunes z stays near 0 whatever the prompts, and the evidence is in the generations and the hottest positions, so ask for generated tokens. Each prompt costs one forward pass per model and each generated token one more: on a CPU, prefer small models and few prompts.

Quantization parameters

GGUF files and bitsandbytes checkpoints are read dequantized to float32, one tensor at a time, so every analysis accepts them. A comparison with a quantized model mixes what fine-tuning changed and what quantization destroyed; the second is measured per tensor as a noise floor.

Table 10 — Quantized and refused formats

Input Reader Status
GGUF, any type the gguf package can dequantize models.gguf_source.GgufSource supported; the Behaviour Probe loads it through transformers
bitsandbytes nf4, fp4 (4-bit) and int8 models.bnb.BnbSource supported, without bitsandbytes
any other quant_method (GPTQ, AWQ, EXL2...) models.detect._classify refused: only bitsandbytes and GGUF
pickle weights .bin, .pt, .pth, .ckpt models.detect._classify refused: unpickling can run code
DoRA, non-LoRA PEFT methods models.lora refused

A tensor whose GGUF type cannot be dequantized fails alone and is noted; Hub Lineage skips repositories with another quantization method and says why.

GGUF file choice

A folder or repository holding several GGUF files asks which one to read, listing them from the most precise. Unattended reads (Hub Lineage children, Provenance candidates, any choice left on auto) take the most precise. Precision is read from the type in the file name, in this order, unknown types last: F32, BF16, F16, Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_K_M, Q5_K_S, Q5_K, Q5_1, Q5_0, Q4_K_M, Q4_K_S, Q4_K, Q4_1, Q4_0, IQ4_XS, IQ4_NL, Q3_K_L, Q3_K_M, Q3_K_S, IQ3_S, IQ3_XXS, Q2_K, IQ2_S, IQ2_XS, IQ2_XXS, IQ1_M, IQ1_S. A GGUF file on the Hub is downloaded whole into the HF cache; safetensors are read by Range.

Q/K permutation in llama-type GGUF

llama.cpp's convert_hf_to_gguf.py permutes the rows of q_proj and k_proj for the architectures deci, granite, granitemoe, llama, interleaving the two rotary halves of every head. GgufSource.load reverses it with unpermute_rows, using the attention.head_count metadata for Q and attention.head_count_kv for K, so tensors line up with the original weights; a row-range read of such a tensor dequantizes it whole first. Names are mapped back through the gguf package's table and a config is rebuilt from the metadata.

bitsandbytes layout

A 4-bit weight is stored as packed codes (two per byte, high nibble first), one absmax scale per block, a 16-value code book (quant_map) and a JSON state (shape, block size, nesting). With double quantization the scales are themselves quantized (nested_absmax, nested_quant_map, offset) and decoded first. The block size comes from the state, with 64 as fallback. An int8 weight has one scale per row (SCB): W = weight × SCB / 127. The result equals bitsandbytes' own dequantization.

Noise floors

models.quant.noise_floor quantizes the base tensor with the compared tensor's scheme and dequantizes it again: the relative error ‖Q(W) − W‖ / ‖W‖ is the change the tensor would show had fine-tuning not touched it. It is measured on 256 evenly spaced rows (all rows of a smaller tensor), because a relative error converges quickly.

Table 11 — Noise floor by scheme

Scheme Floor Method
F32, F64 0 lossless
GGUF types with a Python quantizer (legacy, ternary, F16, BF16) exact gguf.quants.quantize then dequantize
GGUF K- and IQ-quants, other types without one estimated, labelled uniform asymmetric quantizer on blocks of 32
bitsandbytes nf4, fp4 exact block-wise absmax, nearest value of the file's code book
bitsandbytes int8 exact row-wise absmax over ±127 levels

Bit widths used for estimates: Q2_K: 2, Q3_K: 3, Q4_K: 4, Q5_K: 5, Q6_K: 6, Q8_K: 8, IQ1_S: 1, IQ1_M: 1, IQ2_XXS: 2, IQ2_XS: 2, IQ2_S: 2, IQ3_XXS: 3, IQ3_S: 3, IQ4_NL: 4, IQ4_XS: 4, NVFP4: 4; a type missing from this list is estimated at 4 bits. K-quants are somewhat more accurate than the uniform model, so the estimate errs on the high (conservative) side. The double quantization of bitsandbytes scales is not simulated.

analysis.stats.quantization_floor combines the floors of both sides in quadrature when both are quantized, and gives no floor to an adapter compared with its own base (its update is exact). analysis.stats.beyond_noise calls a change real when it exceeds 2 floors and 1e-05, the rounding level; the second condition matters for F16 and BF16, whose floors are tiny.

Table 12 — Where floors are used

Analysis Use
Weight Diff per tensor: floor, exact or estimated, beyond-noise flag; count beyond noise
Token Shifts, Hub Lineage per kept update: floor and beyond-noise flag, with a warning
Provenance none: quantization lowers raw cosines only slightly, thresholds still apply
Behaviour Probe none: the models are compared by their outputs

Never read a raw change of a quantized tensor on its own: a model merged into a 4-bit base and saved again differs on every tensor by about its floor.
